tier_reason: The README's three first-party bar charts (assets/bench_fib_40.png, bench_lar_arr_add.png, bench_member_access.png) show mean times for Type-V, node --jitless and python3 with hardware and runtime versions stated, but the benchmark programs (test.py, test.js and the Type-C sources) are not in the repo and Type-V's build flags and exact CPU model are not stated, so it cannot reach A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mean execution time from the README bar charts: array allocation + sum Type-V 0.828s vs node --jitless 0.892s (about 1.08x faster) and python3 1.307s (about 1.58x faster); fib(40) Type-V 9.91s vs node --jitless 8.32s (about 1.19x slower) and python3 11.07s (about 1.12x faster); member access Type-V 0.689s vs node --jitless 0.494s (about 1.39x slower) and python3 1.164s (about 1.69x faster). All ratios derived from page data.
corrections.caveats: Mixed result: the README only claims Type-V is 'very comparable to node in interpreter mode' and 'beats node on some benchmarks (unpublished)'; the published charts show it ahead of node --jitless only on the array test (about 7%) and slower on fib(40) and member access, while it beats CPython 3.12 on all three tests (1.12x to 1.69x). The baseline is V8 with the JIT disabled (Ignition interpreter only), and the comparison is cross-language (Type-C programs vs hand-written JS and Python equivalents). Numbers exist only in PNG charts; the node fib(40) bar carries a large error bar (roughly 6.6s to 10.1s). The benchmark programs are not published: the type-v repo has no tests directory, and type-c's tests/test1/test.tc is now a unit test, not the fib benchmark. Type-V build flags not stated; CPU is an unnamed AMD EPYC (Family 25, Model 1) VM with 2 vCPUs. The README says the VM is 'very unoptimized', not production ready and not secure; GC limited to about 1MB. Last commit January 2025.

notes: Numbers in the record match the charts exactly; I added the CPython ratios, which are the only consistent win. Kept as a weak flagged C entry: not faster than node --jitless on 2 of 3 tests, benchmark sources unpublished, build flags unstated. License (LICENCE.md, Apache-2.0), 5 stars, last commit 2025-01-29 (stale) all confirmed.

tier_reason: Section 9.1 of the first-party u2 interpreter README gives the wasm3 comparison (geomean 0.5957, median 0.7116 over n=383; ChaCha20, SHA512, BLAKE2s times) with no compiler, flags or exact CPU, and the corpus (/tmp/uwvm2test) and analysis note are not published; the repo's benchmark/ directory covers only the parser and utils (mutex, utf, xxh3) and test/0013.uwvm_int holds correctness tests, so there is no public harness.

corrections.caveats: First-party section 9.1 of the u2 interpreter README, labelled by the authors as 'not universal claims', from a 2026-02 AArch64/Apple Silicon workflow with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated. The 383-module corpus lives in /tmp/uwvm2test and is not published; the cited analysis note test/uwvm2test/u2_vs_wasm3_asm_stitch_analysis.txt returns 404 and the repo's test/ directory has no uwvm2test folder; benchmark/ only covers parser and utility code. The README says memory-heavy and branch-heavy kernels can lose to wasm3 and that u2 trades code size for speed (not a minimal interpreter in the wasm3/WAMR class). Translation-time peepholes that delete const+drop runs and inline trivial calls could flatter microbenchmark modules in the corpus. Not compared with wasmtime, wasmer or WAMR; wasm3 is the only baseline.

notes: All claimed numbers appear verbatim in src/uwvm2/runtime/compiler/uwvm_int/readme.md section 9.1. Metadata confirmed: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE.md), 14 stars, last commit 2026-09-20 (active), not a fork. Shortcomings: unpublished corpus and analysis note, no compiler/flags/CPU model, wasm3 the only baseline.

tier_reason: The README Performance table compares VMIR with LLVM LLI on test/misc/src/sha1test.c (public, as are the VMIR Makefile at -O2 and test/misc/Makefile building bitcode at -O0/-O1/-O2), but the CPU model ('Core i7 3.2GHz'), LLVM/lli version and flags, and which bitcode optimisation level was timed are not stated, so it is first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Core i7 3.2GHz, sha1test over 64MB of random data: VMIR 4.8s vs LLVM LLI 7m 39s (about 96x faster, derived from page data); native 0.39s (VMIR about 12x slower than native, derived from page data). Raspberry Pi 2 (BCM2709): VMIR 1m 42s, VMIR JIT 17.5s, native 3.54s (no LLI figure). README: interpretation is about 10x slower than native on x86.
corrections.caveats: Single README table, one workload (SHA-1), no exact CPU model, no LLVM version or lli flags, and no statement of which bitcode optimisation level (the test Makefile builds -O0, -O1 and -O2) was timed. The 96x gap is against lli's interpreter, which the README itself says 'is not intended to run code fast in any way', so it is a weak baseline; against native code VMIR is about 12x slower on x86 and about 29x slower on the Pi 2 (JIT about 5x slower; derived from page data). The JIT exists only for 32-bit ARM. VMIR also runs WebAssembly but is not compared with wasm3, WAMR or wasmtime. Built-in libc is incomplete, no vector types (code must be compiled with -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize), no C++ STL. Last commit 2018-08-29.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; benchmark source test/misc/src/sha1test.c exists. Kept at C: weak baseline (lli interpreter), no CPU model/compiler versions. Metadata confirmed: MIT (LICENSE, Lonelycoder AB 2016), 700 stars, 80 forks, last commit 2018-08-29 (abandoned), not archived.
